title: Why Moses Raised a Bronze Serpent
paragraphs:
Why Moses Raised a Bronze Serpent
The Scandal in the Wilderness That Pointed to the Cross—and Why God Still Uses Broken Things to Save Broken People
Most people never notice how strange this story really is.
Death moving from tent to tent.
Not a miracle cure poured from heaven.
A bronze serpent lifted high on a pole.
At first glance, it almost feels shocking.
Why would God use the image of the very thing that was killing them?
Why raise it up where everyone could see?
And why would Jesus Himself point directly to this moment when explaining salvation?
This is one of the most overlooked stories in Scripture, yet hidden inside it is one of the most breathtaking pictures of the Gospel ever revealed.
Because the story of the bronze serpent is not ultimately about snakes.
And perhaps more personally, it is about you.

Israel had witnessed miracle after miracle. God had delivered them from Egypt. He had split the sea before them. He fed them with manna from heaven. He guided them by cloud during the day and fire by night.
Yet despite seeing God's faithfulness repeatedly, they became restless.
"Then the people spoke against God and against Moses..." (Numbers 21:5)
Their complaints revealed something deeper than frustration.
The Hebrew word often associated with this kind of rebellion carries the idea of speaking against authority, resisting what God has provided, and rejecting His leadership.
And many of us know exactly what that looks like.
We pray for blessings and then complain when God does not answer quickly enough.
We ask for provision and then despise what He provides.
We beg for guidance and then resist His direction.
The wilderness is not only a place in ancient Israel.
Sometimes the wilderness is inside us.
"Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and many people of Israel died."
The phrase "fiery serpents" comes from the Hebrew word שָׂרָף (saraph).
The venom created an intense burning sensation that eventually led to death.
The people who had complained against God now found themselves face-to-face with their mortality.
Suddenly the issue was no longer discomfort.
And isn't that often how conviction works?
We ignore sin while everything seems manageable.
Then one day we realize the poison has already spread.
The symptoms may differ, but the poison is the same.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." (Romans 3:23)
Including the one reading this article.
The people finally came to Moses and confessed:
Because repentance always begins where excuses end.
God did not pretend the sin never happened.
He did not say judgment was unnecessary.
He did not call evil good.
Yet He also made a way for mercy.
"Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole; and it shall be that everyone who is bitten, when he looks at it, shall live." (Numbers 21:8)
The Hebrew word for bronze is נְחֹשֶׁת (nechoshet).
Interestingly, the Hebrew words for serpent (נָחָשׁ, nachash) and bronze (nechoshet) sound remarkably similar, creating a vivid wordplay familiar to Hebrew readers.
The bronze symbolized what had already been judged.
And anyone who looked upon it in faith would live.
Think about how offensive that must have seemed.
Centuries later, a religious leader named Nicodemus came to Jesus under the cover of darkness.
What Jesus told him forever connected the wilderness to the Cross.
"And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up." (John 3:14)
"And just as Moses lifted up the serpent..."
Jesus was declaring that the bronze serpent was never merely about Israel.
At first this comparison sounds strange.
"He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us..." (2 Corinthians 5:21)
But He willingly took upon Himself the judgment our sin deserved.
"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us."
The bronze serpent represented judged sin.
Jesus became the fulfillment of that picture.
The wrath we deserved fell upon Him.
The judgment we earned landed on Him.
The death that belonged to us was absorbed by Him.
And now anyone who looks to Christ in faith lives.
The Gospel is not fundamentally about what we do for God.
It is about what God has done for us through Jesus Christ.
The Israelites could not remove the poison themselves.
Neither can we remove sin from our own hearts.
The Gospel says look to Christ.
The Cross remains a scandal because it destroys human pride.
Yet salvation comes entirely through grace.
"For by grace you have been saved through faith." (Ephesians 2:8)
Grace means the gift is undeserved.
The bronze serpent story reveals a God who is both just and merciful.
A God who refuses to ignore sin but also refuses to abandon sinners.
Maybe that is why this story resonates so deeply.
Because many of us know what it feels like to carry poison.
Some carry the poison of addiction.
Some carry shame from secret sins.
Mistakes that still whisper at night.
Failures that still haunt the mind.
Yet the Gospel announces something astonishing:
Your story does not have to end where your failure began.
That is why the bronze serpent matters.
It reminds us that God often transforms the very place of our deepest shame into a testimony of His greatest glory.
The wounds become evidence of healing.
The ashes become evidence of restoration.
The scandal becomes evidence of grace.
Perhaps today you feel like one of those Israelites lying in the wilderness.
Aware that you cannot save yourself.
Then hear the invitation of the Gospel.
The One who was lifted up.
The One who bore the curse.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
If your desire is to glorify God through spreading biblical truth, your support helps make that possible.
One look at the serpent saved dying Israelites.
One look at Christ still saves dying souls.
